2. Summary

CKB is still hard to buy or sell for local money. An exchange asks the seller to deposit the coins first. An identity check turns people away. Twine is the other path, and it already trades on testnet. Two people trade directly. The seller locks CKB in their own Fiber channel by paying a hold Twine creates. The buyer pays the seller in local currency, outside Twine. Twine keeps the order book. It can release that hold only by paying the buyer, and it learns the buyer’s secret only from that payment. Twine never holds the cash, and the operator cannot settle that lock into the operator’s own wallet. The operator does decide the dispute. The same person runs the hub and publishes the solver. A seller uses a hub whose solver they trust. A solver key that is also the buyer cannot award that trade.

The hub operator publishes the solver. That solver can pay the buyer or wait for the seller’s channel lock to expire. Orders travel on Nostr. The coins move on Fiber. The Twine daemon does not open or fund channels. A buyer whose Fiber node cannot receive gets inbound from an LSP. There is no open-source LSP for that yet. Milestone 3 builds one. It opens the channel from its own node to any Fiber node, not only Fiber Studio, on testnet, and the channel liquidity is mine. JIT receive inside testnet Cellula stays a collaboration with the Cellula developers and is not part of this grant. This grant finishes the solver app, the rebuilt trading app, the website, and that LSP. Every check during those four months is testnet. When that work is in, the public hub switches to mainnet.

  • Grant Amount Requested: $12,000 USD (payable in CKB at the public CKB/USD rate when each payment is disbursed)
  • ETA to Completion: 4 months from approval
  • CKB Wallet / Funding Address: <Insert CKB address >

3. Project Introduction

The Problem

Buying or selling CKB for local currency today means a centralized exchange or an identity-checked on-ramp. Where those are banned, people still need a way to trade.

  • Deposit first. Centralized P2P desks make the seller send CKB into the desk’s wallet before anyone can buy. A freeze or a hack takes those coins.
  • Identity checks shut people out. KYC ramps collect identity documents and often reject the places where person-to-person trading is how people actually get coins.
  • Exchanges are banned. In some countries a centralized desk is not allowed. People there still need to buy and sell CKB for local money, and the trade left is person to person.
  • That trade has no lock. Someone has to go first. The seller can take the local money and keep the CKB, or the buyer can take the CKB and not pay.
  • A swap cannot pay a bank. On-chain markets such as UTXOSwap move crypto for crypto. They cannot settle a bank transfer, mobile money, or cash.

The Solution

Twine lets a seller and a buyer trade CKB for local currency while the CKB stays in Fiber channels they already control. The buyer pays the seller directly. Twine records the payment method and the clock. It does not hold the cash or process the payment. The beta ran more than 20 testnet trades while bugs were being fixed, so I do not have an exact count.

Why Now?

Fiber hold invoices make this escrow possible with the tools Fiber already ships. Twine adds no custom CKB script. A normal trade window is 48 hours from the lock. A trampoline payout, including a buyer on testnet Cellula, is 68 hours. Those are the clocks Twine enforces. The seller’s channel stays locked until Fiber’s TLC expires. On a testnet Cellula seller that expiry was measured at 64 hours and 132 hours after the lock. The coins return then. The 48-hour and 68-hour numbers are not that measurement.

User Experience

The order book is public Nostr messages. A trader needs a Nostr key, a relay, and their own Fiber wallet.

  • On a computer: Fiber Studio, or any Fiber wallet, pays the lock and receives the CKB. The seller needs a channel that can send. A Fiber node that cannot receive gets inbound from the LSP in Milestone 3. That open is for any Fiber node, not only Fiber Studio. The Twine daemon does not open the channel.
  • On a phone: testnet Cellula pays the lock and receives the CKB. The Cellula wallet is testnet only. twine-app shows the lock as a QR code. The trader pays it from Cellula, or scans it with Fiber Studio on a computer. A Cellula buyer who cannot receive gets inbound from JIT in Cellula. I will build that with the Cellula developers. It is not part of this grant. Until that inbound exists, the daemon keeps payment instructions closed.

4. Team & Roles

Chukwuma Ebube (ebube.dev | GitHub: @chukwuma619) — Lead Developer, and the only person paid by this grant. I am the only maintainer.

I am a software engineer with over five years of experience, building on Nervos CKB. The CKB Community Fund previously funded Fiber Studio under the Fiber Desktop v1 grant. That proposal passed, all three milestones were completed, and the app is still actively maintained. Twine is the next step of that Fiber work: the same hold invoices, used so people can trade CKB for local money.

  • Fiber Studio (getfiberstudio.com | GitHub) — desktop app for a Fiber node. Channels, CKB and UDT payments, and Lightning through a cross-chain hub. Keys stay on the machine.
  • Fiber CCH Hub (GitHub) — self-hosted kit for atomic swaps between Fiber and Bitcoin Lightning.
  • FiberFlow (GitHub) — self-hosted checkout for stores on Fiber. The merchant keeps the wallet key.
  • backr (GitHub) — creator memberships on Nervos CKB, paid over Fiber.
  • ckeeper (GitHub) — a Telegram bot for a CKB wallet: balance, send, and limits in a direct message.

5. Current Status

This is not a paper design. The coordinator, the phone wake-up, the Fiber node package, a proof-of-concept app, and a download site are public and running against testnet. The grant pays for the solver app, the rebuilt trading app, the website, and a testnet LSP. The LSP opens inbound for any Fiber node that cannot receive.

The beta

The beta closed with 100+ downloads and more than 20 testnet trades. Bugs were fixed while those trades were running, so the count is a floor, not an exact ledger. I am not turning the download number into a user count, and I do not have a fiat total for those trades. The community is on Telegram and X.

Testnet beta of twine-app4096×2304 255 KB

Implemented today (in code and on testnet)

  • Trade engine. Live on testnet: sell ads (kind 31420), full or partial takes, a Fiber hold under the buyer’s H(S_b), settle on release. Cancel works only before the seller has paid. The daemon does not open or fund channels.
  • Route gate. A dry-run route check sends no coins. No route means awaiting-route before fiat, or awaiting-invoice if fiat was already marked sent.
  • Clocks. The trade window is 48 hours from the lock, or 68 hours when the buyer invoice is trampoline (testnet Cellula is one). hold_window_end_ms uses the earlier of that window and the inbound TLC expiry, so the trade stops on time even when the TLC is longer. An unpaid hold expires after 1 hour. The buyer can mark the local payment sent only while the hold still leaves 2 hours to release, 4 hours for a dispute, and Fiber’s routing time (at least 30 minutes). After that mark, the seller has 2 hours, then the buyer is asked to dispute. The seller’s CKB stays in the channel until the TLC expires. A testnet Cellula seller measured 64 hours and 132 hours from lock to that expiry. The daemon test already keeps a 132-hour TLC on a 48-hour trade window. Fiber returns the coins at the TLC expiry, not at 48 hours.
  • Disputes. Live when TWINE_SOLVER is set. Kind 31421 names the solver and the 4-hour window. The solver can pay the buyer, record that the buyer did not pay, or record that the money arrived and the CKB could not be delivered. A buyer who never marks the payment sent does not get a public record today. Month 2 publishes that no-show as buyer-unpaid.
  • Public failures. Kind 31422 already publishes fiat-owed, buyer-unpaid, and unresolved. Successful settles are Month 2. The app totals are Month 3.
  • Phone wake. twine-push sends an empty alert. The trade stays in the app.
  • Host install. DEPLOY.md and docker/ run Fiber fnn 0.10.0, the daemon, and push. The coordinator image is Month 2.
  • App. twine-app already posts, takes, chats, attaches a receipt, opens a dispute, and shows the hold as a QR. Android, macOS, Linux, and Windows builds are published. It holds no Fiber key and cannot award. twine-solver is Month 1. Store listing is Month 4.

6. Application Design

Orders and chat are Nostr messages. The coins move on Fiber. Local currency stays outside Twine.

6.1 Functional Overview

Cancel works only while the hold is unpaid. A dispute does not pause the Fiber timelock. A route check is a look, not a reservation. Month 4 puts one trade on an ad and gives each payment method its own window inside the hold.

Trade Sequence

The buyer mints secret S_b on their own Fiber node and builds a payout invoice under H(S_b) (SHA-256). Take carries that invoice. Twine copies the hash onto a hold invoice and stores no preimage. Fiat never touches Twine. The operator learns S_b only when send_payment on the buyer invoice succeeds, then uses that same preimage to settle the hold.

Trade State Machine

Partial takes can share one ad today. Milestone 4 keeps a single trade in flight per ad.

  fiatSent --> disputed: Dispute opened

When fiat was marked sent and the solver window ends with no decision, the trade stays fiat-sent or disputed and the daemon publishes unresolved. Release is refused. The trade window moves the trade to refunding. Fiber moves it to expired when the seller’s TLC expires and the coins come back. On a long seller route that expiry is later than the trade window. A dispute opened before fiat is marked sent still refunds at the fiat deadline. The coins still wait for the TLC.

Fiber team members @ArthurZhang, @quake, @T_Silva and others gave feedback on the Fiber integration. Thanking them here is not an endorsement of this proposal.

6.2 Architecture & Components

No new CKB script. The lock is a Fiber hold invoice on fnn 0.10.0. Kind 31420 is a public ad. Kind 31421 is the hub’s public card. Kind 31422 is a public trade outcome. Kind 4242 is a private action between a trader and the daemon. Kind 4243 is a private chat between the two traders. Traders use their own Fiber wallet. Twine does not ship one. CCC and the Nervos DAO are outside this design. The repositories stay public. Milestone 1 adds the license file.

6.3 Design Rationale

Nostr carries the book, so there is no new on-chain order-book script. Fiber’s hold invoice is the lock: the hash, the timelock, and the refund already ship. The seller’s CKB stays in the channel the seller paid from. Milestone 4 keeps one trade in flight per ad. A partial amount on that one trade stays.

The hold uses the buyer’s payment hash H(S_b). Twine never mints S_b. The operator learns it only when the payout to the buyer succeeds, and only then settles the hold. A retry must reuse that hash. cancel_invoice runs only while the hold is still Open. After the seller has paid, the daemon refuses that call, so the operator cannot hand the coins back early and cannot take them.

The hub can wait out the TLC instead of releasing. It cannot collect the locked CKB without paying the buyer. Local currency is outside Fiber. The hub operator publishes one solver, and on the public hub that solver is me. Traders accept that solver by using the hub. award-buyer pays the buyer. buyer-unpaid, or a window with no decision, leaves the coins until the TLC expires, and the daemon refuses a later release. fiat-owed records that the local money arrived and the CKB could not be delivered. Paying the buyer, or recording fiat-owed, requires this trade’s chat sealed to the solver. The daemon stores that ciphertext and cannot read it. The solver cannot pay a buyer who never sealed the chat. The award is public on kind 31422.

What the seller trusts the operator for. Three things.

  1. The operator’s Fiber node sends the payout when the seller, or the solver, releases. If that node is down, the coins sit until the TLC expires and return to the seller. The buyer who already paid is left with a public note, not the coins.
  2. As the published solver, the operator decides a dispute. A wrong award-buyer sends the seller’s CKB to the buyer. A wrong buyer-unpaid returns the CKB to the seller after the buyer has paid.
  3. The operator keeps the node up until the TLC expires. The operator cannot settle the lock into the operator’s own wallet. The secret comes from paying the buyer.

Trade on a hub whose solver you trust. Anyone can run this software. The solver on a hub is that hub’s operator, named on its kind 31421 card before anyone locks coins. On the public hub that solver is me. A seller who does not trust that person uses another hub, or does not take the ad. The daemon does not fix a bad choice of hub.

If the solver and the buyer are the same key. The daemon checks the seller, then the buyer, then the solver. A message from the buyer’s key is the buyer, even when that key is also TWINE_SOLVER. resolve accepts only the solver, so that key cannot award the trade. The dispute runs out the window, the record is unresolved, and the CKB returns to the seller when the TLC expires. The same check applies if the solver’s key is the seller’s key: they can release, which any seller can do, and they cannot send resolve. The coins still return to the seller if nobody else decides.

If the same person uses two keys. The daemon cannot tell. A solver key can send award-buyer, and the hub pays the other key’s invoice. The daemon also does not refuse a take from the solver key. That is the trust in the previous list. I will not use the solver key to trade on the public hub. A hub that does is a hub to leave.

What “non-custodial” means here. Twine never holds the cash. The seller’s CKB sits in the seller’s channel, locked to the buyer’s secret. The operator cannot spend that lock except by paying the buyer. It does not mean the operator makes no decision. The title stays. This paragraph is the limit on it.

Two clocks. Twine sets the hold invoice’s final_expiry_delta to 48 hours, or 68 hours for a trampoline buyer invoice. That is the trade window. Fiber adds hop time on the seller’s path, and Twine cannot set the TLC expiry that results. hold_window_end_ms ends the trade at the earlier of the trade window and the inbound TLC expiry. The channel unlock is the TLC. Month 2 records locked_at and that TLC expiry on the public trade. The 48-hour and 68-hour claim is the trade window only. A check that measures lock to TLC expiry will show the longer number on a testnet Cellula seller, and that longer number is what the proposal now says.

The fee is one secret and two amounts. There is no second lock the hub can settle first.

6.4 Fee Model & Sustainability

Fees are not charged today. The software still requires the buyer’s invoice to equal the hold. Month 2 adds one coordinator fee, taken only when a trade settles, split across both sides in CKB.

The fee is upkeep for the daemon and hub the trader chose. Anyone who runs a coordinator sets the rate, including 0%.

The seller locks H = principal + seller_fee. The buyer invoice is P = principal - buyer_fee under the same H(S_b). The hub pays P, settles the hold for H, and keeps H - P. The preimage rule is unchanged.

Example (100 CKB principal, 0.5% each side):

  1. The seller locks 100.5 CKB (H). The seller also pays the route fee on that hold. The hub receives the invoice amount, 100.5.
  2. The buyer’s invoice is 99.5 CKB (P), under the same H(S_b).
  3. The hub pays that invoice. send_payment caps the route fee at 0.5% (MAX_FEE_RATE is 5 per thousand). A trampoline payout that uses the cap costs the hub about 0.5 CKB to deliver 99.5, so the hub sends about 100.0.
  4. The hub settles the hold for 100.5. About 0.5 CKB stays in the hub channel, not 1.0.

The 1.0 CKB is H - P before the route fee. On the trampoline path measured in review, 100 in and 100.5 out, the hub’s remainder is the seller’s half. A direct path with a smaller route fee leaves more of the 1.0. I am not raising the rate to cover the route. An operator who wants the full 1.0 after routing sets a higher rate on their own card.

If that fee should leave the hub node, the daemon may send it onward only after the hold is settled, under a new payment hash. The trade is already settled. A failed hop does not reopen the hold.

The rate, including 0%, is on the hub’s public card (kind 31421) before anyone locks coins. The $1,500 infrastructure line is the year the public site and hub run, including updates to that site, whether or not a hub charges a fee. After that year, the fee is how an operator covers the server. The fee does not buy channel liquidity. The CKB in the hub, and the CKB the LSP puts in a channel, are mine.

7. Key Benefits for CKB

This puts CKB in people’s hands through the payment channels Nervos already built.

  • Fiber gets a real payment. Every completed trade is a hold plus a payout, often across more than one hop, for local money a swap cannot settle. People who can buy and sell CKB this way open a channel and use it. That use is what this brings to CKB.
  • Someone else can run it. The coordinator image and the public event kinds are the tooling. Another operator sets their own fee, including 0%.

Months 0 through 4 are built and accepted on testnet. Nothing in those months is a mainnet launch. When the Milestone 4 delivery checks pass, I switch the public hub to mainnet. The 12-month run starts then, on my own CKB, with the payable and receivable amounts published on kind 31421. Store listings during development talk to the testnet hub. After the switch they talk to the mainnet hub. Cellula is testnet only, so it is not part of that switch. The mainnet path on a phone is Fiber Studio. Before I raise that published cap, I review the desk myself. The repositories stay public, so anyone can review them too, including the Nervos team. There is no mainnet pilot in front of the solver.

8. Detailed Deliverables & Milestones

Four months from approval, all of it on testnet. Kickoff, Milestone 1, and Milestone 2 are $2,400 each. Milestone 3, the LSP, is $3,000. Milestone 4 is $1,800. Each payment follows a public progress report on Nervos Talk. I write that report, and each acceptance item is marked done or still open. I do not request the next payment while an acceptance item for the current milestone is still open.

Milestone 1 — Solver app (Month 1)

The daemon already accepts resolve. The trading app can open a dispute and seal the chat. It cannot award, and this month does not add an award screen to it. twine-solver is a separate install from the same Flutter project, for the hub operator.

  • Deliverables:
    • twine-solver. The solver nsec is a different key from any trading identity, in this app’s own keystore, with screenshot blocking on key screens. A QR shows the solver npub to the hub operator. twine-app cannot import that key.
    • One hub and its relays. No order book. Live pending disputes, take one case, and my disputes (in progress / closed). A content-free twine-push wake goes to every configured solver until someone takes the case, then a wake that it was taken.
    • Chat with the buyer and the seller. Read sealed trade evidence when a party shares it.
    • Resolve with award-buyer, buyer-unpaid, or fiat-owed. A locked hold stays off cancel_invoice.
    • Optional read vs read-write: watch the queue, or award.
    • Direct download for the operator. It is not part of the App Store or Play Store submission.
    • License file. An open-source license on the daemon, the app, and the website. twine-solver uses it.
  • Acceptance Criteria:
    • A solver key awards a disputed testnet trade from twine-solver. That key is absent from twine-app, and the trading app has no award action. The daemon does not call cancel_invoice on the received hold.
    • The daemon, app, and website repositories each contain that license file, and twine-solver uses it.

Milestone 2 — Fee, public record, and a hostable coordinator (Month 2)

This month is the daemon work the desk needs before anyone else can host it: a public settle record, a fee that does not put the trade at risk, a lock cap that grows with reputation, maintenance mode, a protocol version, and a Docker image a third party can run. All of it is testnet.

  • Deliverables:
    • Key model before more history is published. Reputation mode keeps a stable identity key and signs each trade with a per-trade key. The record attaches when that identity is revealed. Privacy mode uses a fresh key per trade and shows a blank history. Kind 31422 names the key that owns the record.
    • A new taker cannot lock a large ad for free. The hub publishes new_taker_cap_ckb on kind 31421. A key with no settled trade on this hub, including a privacy-mode key, may have one open lock, and that lock cannot exceed the cap. Each settled trade on this hub doubles the cap, up to the ad. Privacy mode stays on the blank-history cap. It does not wipe it.
    • A no-show is a public record. If the fiat window ends and the buyer never marked the payment sent, the daemon publishes buyer-unpaid. Today that record exists only when the solver writes it.
    • Lock time on the public trade. Kind 31422 carries locked_at and the inbound TLC expiry read from list_channels. The trade window is the earlier of that expiry and locked_at plus 48 hours (68 hours for a trampoline payout).
    • Publish successful settles on kind 31422. Today that kind is fiat-owed, buyer-unpaid, and unresolved.
    • Protocol version on kind 31421 and kind 4242. The shipping app and a newer hub refuse each other on purpose.
    • Coordinator Docker image and docs for a third-party operator. The Fiber image under docker/ is already fnn 0.10.0. Those docs point at Fiber’s admin.backup for the node store. The daemon does not keep a second copy of channel state.
    • Maintenance mode. Block new takes while in-flight holds settle or expire.
    • Coordinator fee, including a rate of 0%. The seller locks the principal plus the seller’s fee. The buyer is paid the principal minus the buyer’s fee, under the same hash. Today payout_invoice_ok rejects a buyer invoice that does not equal the hold. This milestone allows the smaller payout. If testnet cannot settle the larger hold afterward, the report says so, the public hub stays at 0%, and that closes the fee item.
  • Acceptance Criteria: This milestone is paid when the public settle record, the new-taker cap, maintenance mode, and the Docker image pass. The fee item closes on a successful testnet settle or on the written report in the last fee check.
    • A settled testnet trade is a public kind 31422 event that names the record’s owner key, locked_at, and the inbound TLC expiry. A privacy-mode key has no prior record on that hub, and a take above new_taker_cap_ckb is refused. A second open lock from that key is refused.
    • A testnet trade whose buyer never marks fiat sent becomes a public buyer-unpaid record when the fiat window ends.
    • The 100 CKB fee example settles on testnet, or the report leaves the public hub at 0%. The report states the route fee on that payout and the CKB left in the hub channel after it.
    • Maintenance mode blocks new takes and leaves in-flight holds to settle or expire.
    • A third party can deploy the coordinator from the published Docker image and docs.

Milestone 3 — LSP (Month 3)

There is no open-source LSP for a Fiber node that cannot receive. This month builds one. A Fiber node with no inbound asks it for capacity. It opens a channel to that node, funds the inbound side, and stands in until that node can receive. Fiber Studio is one such node. Any other Fiber node can ask for the same open. The check stays on testnet.

  • Deliverables:
    • LSP, testnet. Not part of twine-daemon. A Fiber node with no inbound asks it for a channel. The LSP opens that channel from its own node and funds the inbound side in time for the payout. The same open works for Fiber Studio and for any other Fiber node. The CKB in the channel is mine. This grant does not buy that liquidity. The fee does not buy it either. twine-daemon still only pays the buyer’s invoice. It does not call open_channel. JIT inside testnet Cellula stays with the Cellula developers and is not this item. The LSP code is public, under the same open-source license as the daemon.
  • Acceptance Criteria:
    • On testnet, a Fiber node with no inbound receives a CKB payment after the LSP opens and funds that inbound. A second check uses a node that is not Fiber Studio. The Twine daemon does not call open_channel on that trade.

Milestone 4 — Trading app, website, guides, and store listings (Month 4)

Rebuilds the trading app for iPhone, Android, Mac, Windows, and Linux, against testnet, and ships the public website, the guides, and the store listings. The solver app stays a separate install. The daemon gains three rules: one open trade per ad, a clock per payment method, and hub capacity on kind 31421. UDT markets and market-price ads leave this grant. Cellula, where the app mentions it, is named as testnet only. The testnet checks come first. When they pass, I switch the public hub to mainnet. I run that mainnet hub for 12 months on my own CKB and post a quarterly note.

  • Deliverables:
    • One open trade per ad. The live daemon still takes several slices of one post while CKB remains.
    • Per-rail payment catalog on ads for local-currency methods. Each method has a maximum fiat window that still leaves the 2-hour release grace, the 4-hour solver window, and the Fiber routing buffer. The catalog puts the rail and the clock on the order.
    • Hub capacity on kind 31421. Payable CKB is local_balance minus offered_tlc_balance. Receivable CKB is remote_balance minus received_tlc_balance. Only enabled channels count, and a one-way channel counts only in the direction it allows. A path through other nodes is a separate check. The card also carries a short operator profile and the new-taker cap from Month 2. The app shows that capacity before a take and says whether the path is direct or multi-hop. It also says when the trader’s own wallet has no inbound capacity. The route check after the hold locks still opens the payment instructions.
    • Rebuild of twine-app on the live trade flow. Chat, dispute open, and the trader keystore stay. No solver key. Adds filters and the counterparty’s public record. The trade screen shows the trade window and the TLC expiry from Month 2. This month produces the builds submitted to the stores. Those builds talk to a testnet hub until the mainnet switch.
    • Aggregates in the client, from kind 31422: settled count, completion rate, median time to pay, median time to release.
    • Fixed-price ads. Trust shown on a counterparty is the settle record.
    • twine-web: guides and help, a live kind 31420 book, and a directory of hubs from kind 31421 capacity and health. The site today is the download page.
    • Relay failover, and maker relay lists (NIP-65), so one dead relay does not hide the book.
    • Ad expiry on the daemon clock for maker posts that are not refreshed, plus a NIP-40 expiration tag. The daemon clock is the authority. NIP-40 is still a draft, and a relay may keep the event.
    • Hub health on the same 31421 event: Fiber RPC reachable, channels open, a recent payout-path dry-run succeeded, relays reachable. Refresh it on a clock. Capacity is the hub capacity added in this milestone.
    • Operator metrics from the daemon: RPC errors, stuck phases, relay lag. Traders see the Nostr health event. The operator uses the logs.
    • Submit the rebuilt trading app to Google Play and the Apple App Store. Those filings need a D-U-N-S number, and getting that number means applying for the documents first. That cost comes out of the infrastructure line. twine-solver stays a direct download. Direct downloads of the trading app stay available for Android, desktop, and iOS TestFlight.
  • Acceptance Criteria: This milestone is paid when the rebuilt app, the site, the store filings, and the mainnet switch pass.
    • cargo test passes, including one in-flight trade per ad.
    • A kind 31421 event shows payable and receivable CKB from the hub’s own channels, plus the operator profile.
    • Two local-currency methods on an ad each carry their own fiat window inside the trade window (48 hours plain, 68 hours trampoline). The trade screen shows that window and the TLC expiry.
    • A testnet CKB trade completes on a mobile build and a desktop build of the rebuilt app, using the same Nostr key.
    • The order book can filter, and the counterparty screen shows settled count, completion rate, and the two medians computed from kind 31422.
    • twine-web shows the guides, the live kind 31420 book, and a hub directory whose capacity and health match kind 31421.
    • With one configured relay down, the book still loads from another.
    • Google Play and App Store submissions are filed (in review or live). The listing text says the wallet path through Cellula is testnet.
    • After those testnet checks, the public kind 31421 card names the mainnet Fiber node. The site book follows that card. Cellula is not on this hub.

After this grant

Worth doing once the desk has real use. The lock stays one secret created by the buyer, and each hub keeps one published solver. None of this is part of the $12,000.

  • twine-cli. A terminal trader and solver over Nostr, so someone can trade without the app. The app already trades without it. It holds no Fiber key. It is built once the desk has real use.
  • Review before the cap goes up. The switch at the end of Milestone 4 opens the desk. The cap on kind 31421 stays the CKB I fund until I have reviewed the desk myself. Anyone can review the same code, including the Nervos team. This grant does not hire an audit firm.
  • JIT stays out of the Twine daemon. An earlier Twine build opened a private one-way channel from the hub when the buyer could not receive. That came out. The hub would have been the liquidity provider, and every wallet would have had to auto-accept a channel this desk opened. The LSP in Milestone 3 is the replacement. It opens inbound for any Fiber node, not only Fiber Studio. I will work with the Cellula developers on JIT receive in testnet Cellula. That Cellula work is outside this $12,000.
  • Whitelisted UDT markets, one asset per channel, on testnet. A mainnet UDT market still waits until public Fiber channels hold that token.
  • Market-price ads, with a fiat premium or discount against a CKB/fiat rate the hub publishes.
  • Maker-defined shorter fiat timers inside the hub’s hold envelope. The per-method windows in Milestone 4 come first.
  • Buy-side maker ads (“want to buy CKB”). The trade hold still uses a buyer-minted payout hash.
  • A dispute assistant in a separate process. It never moves funds and never awards. It uses a read-only solver key, and the daemon rejects resolve from that key.
  • Reputation federation across hubs a client already trusts.
  • Mainnet fee defaults and rate limits on the public book.
  • Routing and client extras: hop_hints, websocket updates with polling kept as the fallback, encrypted Blossom receipts, NIP-59 gift wrap, content-free Web Push, external signers (NIP-46, NIP-07, NIP-55), an optional profile, optional NIP-13 proof of work, and NIP-51 mute lists.

9. Budget Breakdown

$12,000, at the public CKB/USD rate when each payment is disbursed. Kickoff, Milestone 1, and Milestone 2 are $2,400 each. Milestone 3 is $3,000. Milestone 4 is $1,800. Development is my time, on testnet. The CKB the LSP puts in a channel, and the CKB in the mainnet hub, are outside this budget. The fee does not buy that liquidity. I review the desk myself. A hired audit firm is not in this budget. During the 12 months I run the public mainnet hub, I post a short note on Nervos Talk each quarter.

Category Amount Scope Covered
Development $10,376 Core daemon updates, rebuilt twine-app, the separate twine-solver app, twine-web, and the testnet LSP in Milestone 3. UDT, market-price ads, and Cellula’s own JIT are not in this line.
Infrastructure $1,500 The year the public site and hub run. That covers the machine, keeping the site updated through that year, the documents required to get a D-U-N-S number for the store applications, and miscellaneous.
App Store Fees $124 Apple Developer Program, $99 for one year. Google Play Console, $25 once. Renewing Apple after that year is on me.
Total $12,000

10. Out of Scope

This grant pays for the milestones above.

  • A bank connection, custodial fiat, KYC, star ratings, or a legal opinion. Local-currency rules differ by country.
  • DAO-funded channel liquidity. I fund the public hub, and I fund the CKB the LSP places in a channel. The daemon does not open, fund, or rebalance channels. Milestone 3 pays for building the LSP, not for the coins in it. The fee does not buy that liquidity. JIT inside testnet Cellula stays with the Cellula developers.
  • A Fiber node or Fiber key inside either app.
  • A mainnet trade as a paid check during development. The switch happens once the testnet work is in.
  • A mainnet UDT market, UDT in this grant, market-price ads, concurrent trades on one ad, a hired audit firm, and hosting after those 12 months.
  • The feature backlog under “After this grant.”

11. Risks & Mitigations

Risk Mitigation
The other person disappears after the coins are locked The trade window stops the trade at 48 hours, or 68 hours for a trampoline payout (testnet Cellula). The CKB returns when the TLC expires, which on a testnet Cellula seller was 64 hours and 132 hours. From Month 2, a buyer who never marks the payment sent is a public buyer-unpaid record.
Someone tries to cancel a funded lock cancel_invoice is allowed only while the hold is unpaid. After that it is refused.
Local payment is slower than a crypto transfer The lock leaves 2 hours to release, 4 hours to dispute, and time to route. Month 4 gives each payment method its own window inside that lock.
A new buyer has no inbound capacity Payment instructions stay closed until a route exists. The Twine daemon does not open the channel. Milestone 3’s LSP opens inbound for any Fiber node that cannot receive, with my CKB. A testnet Cellula buyer gets inbound from JIT in Cellula, built with the Cellula developers, outside this grant. The buyer then sends the same invoice again. A missing route after fiat is marked sent keeps the report.
The seller takes the money and will not release The buyer seals the chat to the published solver. That solver can pay the buyer, record that the buyer did not pay, or record that the money arrived and the CKB could not be delivered. The solver cannot pay a buyer who never sealed the chat.
The published solver awards the wrong party Traders accept that solver by using the hub. The award is public on kind 31422.
One maintainer I am the only person on this grant. The repositories stay public. A missed month is reported on Talk before the next payment is requested.
A taker locks the seller and walks away After the seller pays, cancel is refused, and the lock costs the taker nothing. From Month 2 a key with no settled trade on this hub, including privacy mode, gets one lock up to the published cap. The cap doubles with each settle on this hub.
The phone wake depends on FCM The alert carries no trade content. The trade still completes in the app if the push does not arrive.
The coins cannot reach the buyer after the money was sent The buyer retries under the same secret. An expired request refunds the seller. A confirmed fiat leg is published as fiat-owed.
The desk cannot send or receive enough CKB Kind 31421 publishes those limits before anyone locks. Twine does not move channel funds to invent a route.
App store review takes time Month 4 files the store submissions and also ships direct downloads and TestFlight. twine-solver is a direct download.
Fiber cannot settle the larger lock after the smaller payout If testnet cannot do it, the report leaves the hub at 0%. The hub is still paid only by paying the buyer.
The book is empty I am the first seller, with my own CKB. On testnet through development, then on the mainnet hub after the switch. Milestone 2’s image is how a second coordinator appears.
A milestone is read as a mainnet launch Months 0 through 4 are accepted on testnet. The public hub switches to mainnet when the Milestone 4 checks pass. The 12 months after that are the hub I run. Cellula stays testnet only.

12. Closing

Twine already trades CKB for local money on testnet. This grant is $12,000 over four months of testnet work, then a switch of the public hub to mainnet. Kickoff, Milestone 1, and Milestone 2 are $2,400 each. The LSP is $3,000. The last milestone is $1,800. The work finishes the solver app, the rebuilt trading app, the website, and a testnet LSP for any Fiber node that cannot receive.

I welcome comments on the solver model and on the fee. Questions are welcome. I appreciate your consideration.

posts.name: Ebube Chukwuma
posts.cooked:
@T_Silva sent this in a DM, so the thread never had it. I am edited the proposal to answer it. This is the feedback, and what I changed.

A new buyer has no inbound CKB. The daemon does not open or fund a channel. An earlier build did open a one-way channel from the hub at release. That came out. Milestone 4 builds a Fiber Studio LSP. It opens the inbound channel from its own node, on testnet, and the CKB in that channel is mine. The grant pays for building the LSP, not for the coins. JIT receive inside testnet Cellula is a collaboration I will do with the Cellula developers. Cellula has not signed onto that, and it is not part of this $15,000. Until a route exists, payment instructions stay closed.

What “non-custodial” means. Twine never holds the cash. The seller’s CKB sits in the seller’s channel, locked to a secret the buyer minted. The daemon learns that secret only when the payout to the buyer succeeds, so the operator cannot settle the lock into the operator’s own wallet. The operator is the solver, and the operator does decide the dispute.

A solver key that is also the buyer cannot award that trade. The daemon checks the seller, then the buyer, then the solver, and resolve accepts only the solver. The window ends unresolved, and the CKB returns when the TLC expires.

Two keys are different. The daemon cannot tell they are the same person. A solver key can send award-buyer, and the hub pays the other key’s invoice. The daemon also does not refuse a take from the solver key. I will not use the solver key to trade on the public hub. A hub that does is a hub to leave. A seller uses a hub whose solver they trust. The solver is named on that hub’s kind 31421 card before anyone locks coins. On the public hub that solver is me.

The lock is longer than 48 hours. 48 hours is the trade window. A trampoline payout, including a buyer on testnet Cellula, is 68 hours. Those are the clocks the daemon enforces. The seller’s channel stays locked until Fiber’s TLC expires. On the testnet Cellula seller in this review, that expiry was 64 hours and 132 hours after the lock. Those two numbers are that measurement. The coins return then. Month 2 records locked_at and the inbound TLC expiry on the public trade.

Mainnet. Development stays on testnet for all four months. The public hub switches to mainnet when the Milestone 4 checks pass: the site, the store filings, the LSP, and the switch. Cellula is testnet only and is not part of the switch. The phone path on mainnet is Fiber Studio. The desk opens at the cap I fund. Before I raise that published cap, I review the desk myself. The repositories stay public, so anyone can review them too, including the Nervos team. This grant does not hire an audit firm, and I am not saying the Nervos team has agreed to review it.

Demand. The beta closed with 100+ downloads and more than 20 testnet trades. Bugs were fixed while those trades were running, so that count is a floor, not a ledger. I am not turning the downloads into a user count, and I do not have a fiat total.

A taker can lock the seller and walk away. After the seller pays, cancel is refused. Today a silent no-show is not a public record. buyer-unpaid is written only when the solver records it. Month 2 publishes buyer-unpaid when the fiat window ends and the buyer never marked the payment sent. The same month caps a new taker: a key with no settled trade on this hub, including privacy mode, gets one open lock, up to the published new_taker_cap_ckb. Each settled trade on this hub doubles the cap, up to the ad.

The money. The ask stays $15,000. Kickoff and milestones 1 to 3 are $3,000 each. Milestone 4 is $2,000 when the site, the store filings, the LSP, and the mainnet switch pass, and $1,000 after the mainnet kind 31421 card has kept refreshing for 6 months. Apple is $99 for one year and Google Play is $25 once, so the store fees are $124. Development is $13,376. The $1,500 is the year the public site and hub run: the machine, updates to the site through that year, the documents I have to file to get a D-U-N-S number for the store applications, and miscellaneous. UDT markets and market-price ads leave this grant. The CKB in the hub, and the CKB the LSP places in a channel, are mine.

The fee. The rate stays 0.5% each side. send_payment caps the route fee at 0.5%. On a 100 CKB trade the seller locks 100.5 and the buyer invoice is 99.5. If the trampoline payout uses that cap, the hub sends about 100.0 to deliver 99.5 and keeps about 0.5 of the 100.5. The 1.0 is H − P before the route fee. The 100 in, 100.5 out figure is the route fee measured in this review. A cheaper route leaves more of the 1.0. I am not raising the rate to cover it.

Nice work, ebubedev. Using Fiber hold invoices without a custom script is a clean design.

One idea on the solver: today the hub operator is a single point of trust (and arguably control) for disputes. Have you considered splitting the dispute key k-of-n across independent node operators? The seller could split the preimage among, say, 3-of-5 solvers. Normal trades never touch them, and in a dispute a quorum must agree. With PTLCs on Fiber later, threshold Schnorr (FROST) would make this cleaner, since no party ever knows the full secret.

I’m building CSR (CKB Service Runner), a sidecar that lets CKB node operators run paid services next to their node, with staked, ranked operators. A threshold-solver service for Twine could be a good fit, and I’d be happy to explore it.

Questions:
Have you looked at the regulatory side? Under the EU’s MiCA rules, a hub operator who charges the 0.5% fee and alone holds the dispute key could be treated as a crypto-asset service provider, which would be hard for a single desk to comply with. Splitting the key across independent operators might help there too.

posts.name: Ebube Chukwuma
posts.cooked:
1. Does a commercial project have no business model, and why start it?

It has one. A coordinator fee, 0.5% on each side, taken in CKB only when a trade settles. It is not charged today. After the first year of the public hub, that fee is how the operator pays for the server and provide liquidity. Anyone who runs a hub sets their own rate, including 0%. I started it so someone can buy or sell CKB for local money without sending the coins to an exchange. The seller’s CKB stays in their own Fiber channel. The local money goes straight to the seller.

2. What does this bring to CKB?

More reason to use Fiber. Every settled trade is a hold and a payout on Fiber, for local money a swap cannot settle. If people can buy and sell CKB this way, more of them open a channel and use it. That use is what gives CKB value here. The lock is a Fiber hold invoice Fiber already ships. The code is public. Anyone can read it and host their own hub.

3. Why this amount?

The amount is the work that has to be built before this works. The solver app, so a dispute can be decided. The trading app, rebuilt for phone and desktop. The website and the store listings. The LSP, because a buyer with no channel open cannot receive. There is no open-source LSP for that yet. This grant builds one. It opens the inbound for any Fiber node, not only Fiber Studio, and stands in until that node can receive.

The CLI is not required for that. It is a terminal client, so someone can trade without the app and giving ai agent access. The app already trades without it. I will take twine-cli out of this grant and build it later when we would have had tractions, and I will update the proposal so the amount matches what is left.

posts.name: Ebube Chukwuma
posts.cooked:
Understood, and I completely agree with that principle—the Community Fund should support builders who are genuinely committed to growing the ecosystem, not quick grant-chasing or hollow consensus.

Just to share a bit of context on my commitment here: I’ve been actively building on Nervos CKB for close to a year now. Beyond Fiber Studio (which I continue to maintain after completing its grant), I’ve built and open-sourced tools like Fiber CCH Hub, FiberFlow, backr, and many others not listed here, alongside contributing code to other projects in the ecosystem and speaking at the last CKCon26.

Twine is a continuation of that work—it already has a working testnet beta with real trades, alongside an active X community and Telegram group where we engage with users and provide hands-on support. My goal is to ship sustainable, open-source P2P and LSP infrastructure that adds lasting utility to Fiber.

What I’m asking for is support to keep the momentum going while growing the product.

I genuinely welcome technical feedback, critical questions, and open discussion from everyone here so we can make sure this is built right.

posts.name: Ebube Chukwuma
posts.cooked:
Our operational and user-growth plan focuses on removing Fiber onboarding friction and targeting communities that actively need P2P ramps:

1. Targeting Markets Where P2P Is a Necessity

Instead of competing with centralized exchanges where they are already convenient, our primary rollout targets regions where CEXs are restricted, banking rails are fragmented, or strict KYC blocks everyday users from buying CKB. In these markets, non-custodial P2P via mobile money, local bank transfers, and cash solves an immediate, real-world problem.

2. Removing Onboarding Friction (LSP + Mobile Wallets)
The biggest barrier to using Fiber today is channel setup and inbound liquidity. Through Milestone 3 (our open-source LSP) and our collaboration with Cellula (JIT inbound liquidity on mobile), a new user won’t need to understand channel management just to buy CKB—they can scan a QR code from their phone or desktop and receive CKB directly.

3. Plugging Into Existing Nervos & Nostr Channels

  • Existing Fiber users: Integrating smoothly with Fiber Studio (which already has an active user base) and Cellula gives existing Nervos users an immediate place to use their channels.

  • Nostr network effect: Because Twine’s order book runs on public Nostr relays rather than a closed database, liquidity and offers are naturally discoverable across the Nostr ecosystem, not just inside a single app.

4. Ongoing Hub Operations & Community Support

After mainnet launch, I will continue running the public hub, maintaining the solver, and handling dispute resolution (backed by the 48–68 hour hold-invoice safety windows), while actively onboarding initial liquidity makers through our existing Telegram groups and X accounts so buyers always have live offers to match with.

Twine is meant to be an active, everyday utility for Fiber—not a repo left sitting on GitHub. If you have suggestions on specific communities or liquidity incentives we should explore, I’d love to hear them!

posts.name: Ebube Chukwuma
posts.cooked:
Clarifying Key Details on Twine: Dispute Protection, LSP Liquidity & Hub Compliance

1. How Buyers Recover Value if CKB Delivery Fails After Fiat Payment

Because fiat moves peer-to-peer outside Twine (via bank transfer, mobile money, or cash), Twine cannot reverse a bank transaction directly—instead, the seller’s CKB is cryptographically locked up front before the buyer ever sends fiat:

  • Pre-Locked Hold Invoice: Before a trade begins, the seller locks the CKB in their own Fiber channel by paying a hold invoice created by Twine. The seller cannot pull those coins back while the trade window is active.

  • Dispute Resolution & Solver Payout: If the buyer sends the local currency (with proof of payment) and the seller disappears or refuses to confirm, the buyer opens a dispute within the trade clock (48 hours for standard trades, 68 hours for trampoline/mobile payouts).

  • Cryptographic Enforcement: The hub operator reviews the payment evidence and instructs the solver to release the hold by paying the CKB directly to the buyer’s Fiber invoice. Crucially, the solver is cryptographically constrained—it can only pay the buyer or let the lock expire back to the seller; the hub operator cannot sweep the locked CKB into their own wallet.

  • Inbound Liquidity & Offline Buyers (LSP): In Milestone 3, our open-source LSP opens inbound channels for buyers on the fly and can use a hold-invoice buffer (bounded safely inside Fiber’s 4-hour default per-hop tlc_expiry_delta / 64–132 hour multi-hop TLC window) to hold the payout until an offline buyer comes back online. Until inbound liquidity is confirmed, the daemon keeps payment instructions closed so a buyer isn’t prompted to send fiat without a valid receiving path.

2. Regulatory Obligations for Hubs That Charge Fees

Twine is designed specifically to minimize custodial and payment-processing risk, though operators must still comply with their local laws:

  • Non-Custodial Architecture: A Twine hub never holds fiat and never takes custody of user CKB. Orders travel over public Nostr relays, fiat moves directly between buyer and seller, and CKB moves directly over Fiber payment channels using native hold invoices. Even in a dispute, the operator only provides an oracle/arbitration signature—they never control the funds.

  • Jurisdictional Responsibility: Because Twine is open-source software, anyone can run a hub. While non-custodial coordination software typically avoids money-transmitter classification in many jurisdictions (since it never holds or transmits user funds), regulatory rules vary by country—especially if a hub operator charges a coordination/arbitration fee or provides commercial LSP liquidity.

  • Operator Compliance: Any individual or entity running a commercial hub or LSP is responsible for assessing and complying with the tax, business registration, or VASP/local regulations in their own jurisdiction, and can set their own relay/hub policies accordingly.

Yes, you’ve got the flow right—it works just like standard P2P on Binance or Bybit, except Twine never touches the fiat or takes custody of the CKB:

  • How the Fiat Moves (Normal Person-to-Person Transfer): Twine does not integrate with banks or process fiat payments. Just like any P2P platform, the buyer simply sends a normal bank transfer, mobile money transfer, or cash directly to the seller’s account outside Twine. Because it’s a standard person-to-person transfer between two individuals, the bank only sees a regular transfer between two accounts—no special bank integration or permission is needed.

  • Currency Agnostic From Day One: Because Twine never touches the cash, we aren’t restricted to starting with a single currency. Any buyer and seller anywhere in the world can trade in whatever local currency and payment method they both use (bank transfer, mobile money, cash, etc.).

  • Where Fiber Comes In (The Escrow): Instead of depositing CKB into a centralized exchange wallet, the seller locks CKB in their own Fiber channel via a hold invoice. Once the seller confirms they received the local transfer in their bank or mobile wallet, the hold settles and the CKB goes straight to the buyer’s Fiber channel. You can read more about the technical flow and our building journey in the earlier POC thread here: Twine: Buy and Sell CKB Without Depositing on an Exchange (Fiber P2P PoC)

  • AML & Local Regulations: Because Twine is non-custodial coordination software—never holding fiat, never holding CKB, and never acting as a financial intermediary—users simply transact peer-to-peer using their own accounts and remain responsible for following their own local banking and tax rules.

About half an hour after the discussion-phase result was announced (Nov 24, 18:21 UTC+8), a community member asked about several new accounts that liked this proposal on the final day of the window.

I reviewed the likes with forum admin data. Three of the liking accounts were registered from one network address within five hours, and each liked within 81 seconds of registering. Nothing in the data links them to the proposal author.

Under the practice of t/7707 and t/10453, their likes would be removed, which would leave 29 of the announced 32, one short of the threshold. The concern was raised after the result was announced, and the t/10453 review treats a proposal whose window closed without such a concern as settled.

[DIS] Werra: Building Trust Infrastructure for Creator Commerce

This audit was initiated solely because a specific, evidenced concern was raised about this proposal while it was in its discussion window. It does not create a standing or proactive audit, and it places no obligation on the coordinator — or anyone else — to screen other proposals for the same patterns.

The announced result therefore stands, and the proposal can proceed to the Metaforo vote.

The committee has been informed, and the full record is kept on file.
